Research dossier · Route A locked · Aug 2026

Visualize Sound

Printing sound on paper as a phase-aware color spectrogram, and getting the sound back with a camera — with numbers to prove how well it survives the trip.

phase 0°the working motif: phase becomes huephase 360°

Verdict: green light. The digital version of this idea (sound → reversible color image) already exists as a 2019 patent. The physical version — print it, scan it, recover the audio, measure the damage — has no rigorous academic treatment. That gap is the paper.

01 · The question

What this research asks

A sound clip is a one-dimensional signal: one long list of amplitude values over time. An image is a two-dimensional grid with color at every cell. The original intuition behind this project was twofold:

  • Can a sound be turned into an image in a mathematically principled way — not by chopping the timeline at arbitrary points — such that the image is genuinely reversible back to sound?
  • If yes, can that image survive the physical world: printed on real paper, photographed with a real phone camera, and still be turned back into recognizable audio?

The first question turns out to be solved (see §03). The second is the open one, and the one this project now pursues:

Research question. How much audio quality survives when a phase-aware color spectrogram is pushed through the print–scan channel, and which encoding choices (color space, channel assignment, resolution, error protection) make it survive best?

02 · Foundations

The math that is already done for us

No new mathematics is required anywhere in this project. Two standard tools do all the heavy lifting.

STFT: the linear-to-matrix answer

The Short-Time Fourier Transform slides a window along the audio, takes a Fourier transform of each windowed slice, and stacks the results side by side. The output is a matrix X[f, t] — one row per frequency, one column per moment in time. This is the principled linear-to-2D conversion: the two axes mean something physical (frequency and time), the trade-off between them is governed by a known law (time–frequency uncertainty: bigger window = finer frequency, coarser time), and the transform is invertible. In code it is one library call (librosa.stft).

Complex numbers as color

Each cell of the STFT matrix is a complex number carrying two facts: magnitude (how loud that frequency is at that moment) and phase (where in its cycle the wave is). An ordinary grayscale spectrogram throws the phase away — which is exactly why naive spectrogram inversion sounds robotic. Keeping the phase is what makes true reversibility possible, and phase is naturally circular (0° = 360°), which is why a circular color dimension — hue — is its natural home. This was the project's founding instinct, and the literature confirms it is the right one.

Hue

Phase

Circular quantity onto circular color dimension. 0–360° maps directly.

Value

Log magnitude

Loudness in dB, matching how hearing works and maximizing dynamic range.

Saturation

Reliability

Fixed, or used as a confidence / signal-presence mask.

Alpha

Open slot

Underused in all prior work. Candidate: onset strength or redundancy for error recovery.

A side note on an early idea: Fourier epicycles (rotating circles that draw shapes) are a different technique — they draw pictures from closed curves and are not needed here. The circular-color instinct was correct; the epicycle machinery is not the vehicle for it.

03 · Prior work

What already exists, honestly mapped

The digital half of the idea has real prior art. Knowing it precisely is what lets this paper position itself as an extension rather than a rediscovery.

WorkWhat it didWhat it did not doStatus
US Patent 10,341,795 (2019) "Log complex color": amplitude as brightness, phase as hue. Claims full recovery of original sound from the image, down to phase. Digital pixels only. Never printed, never scanned, no degradation study. Patent, not paper
PhonoPaper (2014) App that prints a grayscale spectrogram and resynthesizes it live from a phone camera. Proof the physical loop can close. Magnitude only — no phase, so output is a lo-fi "silhouette." No error correction, no metrics, no publication. Demo, not science
HSV-phase CNN work (IEEE 2021) Encodes STFT phase via the HSV color model into RGB images to improve acoustic classification with CNNs. Objective is classifier accuracy, not human viewing, not reversibility, not print. Adjacent
Audio-to-image encodings for CNNs (arXiv 2023–25) Various schemes packing audio features into RGB channels for deep learning pipelines. Same: digital-only, classification-oriented. Adjacent
StegaStamp (CVPR 2019) Deep-learned encoding of data into printed photos, robust to real print + camera capture. 268+ citations — proof the print–scan channel is a respected research problem. Capacity is 56 bits — a hyperlink, not audio. Method inspiration
High-capacity color barcodes (IEEE TIP 2011) Data through print–scan via CMY colorant channels and orientation modulation. Gives citable capacity baselines for paper as a data medium. Generic data, not audio; not human-viewable. Baseline source
Sonorine recovery (arXiv 2020) Recovered 1900s audio from physical cards using photography and computer vision. Historical media recovery, not a designed encoding. Precedent
Kodak-era printed-audio patents (2005–2013) Encode audio bitstreams into printed regions of photographs. Pre-smartphone, pre-deep-learning, no modern evaluation, never entered research literature. Historical
This project Phase-aware color spectrogram through real print and real scan, with quantified recovered-audio quality. — The gap

The positioning sentence for the paper, in one breath: prior work shows sound encodes reversibly into digital color images; we ask whether that reversibility survives the physical print–scan channel, and we engineer and measure an encoding for exactly that.

04 · Proposed system

The Route A pipeline

Design decisions to make (these are the paper's contributions)

  • Channel assignment under print distortion. Printers and cameras damage hue, saturation, and brightness differently. Whether phase belongs in hue (elegant) or brightness (possibly more robust) is an open empirical question — nobody has measured it. This is the core experiment.
  • The alpha / fourth channel. Prior work uses three channels at most. A fourth slot can carry redundancy (a checksum stripe, a low-res backup of magnitude) to aid recovery — printed as a separate visible strip since paper has no alpha.
  • Calibration furniture. Corner fiducial markers for perspective rectification, plus a printed color reference strip so the decoder can undo each printer's specific color shift. Standard tools (OpenCV, ArUco markers) exist for all of it.
  • Resolution and capacity. How many seconds of audio fit on one A4 page at 300 dpi, at what quality? The honest expectation: seconds to tens of seconds of low-bandwidth audio. That is fine — stating the measured capacity limit is a result.
  • Graceful degradation. The analog nature is a feature: unlike a QR code, a damaged spectrogram image degrades smoothly instead of failing entirely. Worth demonstrating explicitly (crumple test, partial occlusion).

05 · Experiments

Measurement plan

Everything below is engineering plus measurement — no new theory. Equipment: a home inkjet or office laser printer, plain and photo paper, a phone camera. Total cost near zero.

PhaseQuestionMethod
E0 · Digital baselineHow much is lost before paper is even involved?Encode → PNG → decode, no printing. Sweep bit depth (8 vs 16), image resolution, STFT window sizes. This reproduces and quantifies what the 2019 patent only claims.
E1 · Channel robustnessWhere should phase live?Same clips encoded with phase-in-hue vs phase-in-brightness vs grayscale-magnitude-only (PhonoPaper-style baseline). Print, scan, decode, compare PESQ/STOI.
E2 · Channel conditionsHow do real-world conditions hurt?Grid over: printer type, paper type, dpi, camera distance and lighting, flatbed scan vs handheld photo.
E3 · StressDoes it degrade gracefully?Crumpled paper, photocopy-of-a-printout, partial occlusion, low light. Plot quality vs damage.
E4 · Content typesWhat survives best?Speech, music (the Mozart figure lives here), environmental sound, an infant cry sample. Different spectral structures, different survival.

Metrics

  • PESQ and STOI — standard perceptual quality and intelligibility scores, computed by comparing recovered audio against the original. Library calls, no math required by hand.
  • Log-spectral distance — how far the recovered spectrogram drifted.
  • Capacity — seconds of audio per A4 page at a stated quality floor.
  • Optional: word error rate of a speech recognizer on recovered speech — an intuitive, brutal intelligibility test.

06 · Results so far

What the code actually shows

These come from a working implementation (STFT codec, HSV encoder, a simulated print-and-capture channel), run on real test clips including recorded speech. The print-scan numbers are from a simulation of ink spread, colour loss, and camera noise — not a real printer yet. They exist to tell the physical experiment where to aim, not to replace it.

The strip problem, fixed

The first working version encoded sound the same way every audio editor already does: one axis frequency, one axis time, producing a long thin strip rather than a genuine matrix. That defeats the original goal of a picture, not a printout of a timeline. The fix is a Hilbert space-filling curve: it visits every cell of a square exactly once, never jumps, and keeps sequence-neighbours physically adjacent on the page. Verified by construction — every one of its steps moves to an adjacent cell, with zero exceptions across curves up to 1024 cells.

Fig. — the same 5.9 s of speech, folded onto a square page. Left: serpentine wrap (cuts visible as clean horizontal bands where each row ends). Right: Hilbert curve (no cut points; sequence-neighbours stay spatially adjacent, visible as blocky rather than striped texture). Both decode back to the original audio exactly — a layout is a permutation, not a loss.

4.59

4.59

Identical to two decimal places, as required. What changes between layouts isn't fidelity — it's how damage spreads across the page, which is the open question the physical experiment will test: a scratch on a strip can sever two moments seconds apart, while a scratch on a Hilbert layout stays local in time.

Digitally, phase-as-hue is close to transparent

Round-tripped through a real 8-bit PNG with no printing involved, keeping phase in hue beats throwing it away by a wide margin — confirming the founding instinct, and reproducing what the 2019 patent only claimed.

Phase collapses first when the channel gets involved — the central finding

The gallery above already hints at the problem: raw phase changes almost randomly between neighbouring time-frequency bins, so hue is pixel-level noise. That is exactly the kind of fine colour detail a printer and camera destroy first. Simulating the channel (ink spread, chroma subsampling, tone shift, sensor noise) confirms it — and the result inverts completely from the digital case.

1.17
phase-as-hue PESQ, light damage
3.33
grayscale PESQ, light damage

Fig. — PESQ of recovered speech across four levels of simulated channel damage, one spectrogram bin per pixel. Phase-carrying schemes (hsv, ifreq) collapse under even light damage; magnitude-only degrades gracefully because it never depended on fine colour detail in the first place.

Listen — after simulated print + camera damage (speech, moderate level)

hue = phase, moderate damage (PESQ 1.06)

grayscale, moderate damage (PESQ 2.59)

A standard phase-vocoder fix was tried — encoding phase as its frame-to-frame deviation rather than its raw value, which is smooth for tonal sound (confirmed: 43% smoother by a measured hue-roughness metric). It didn't rescue quality: the decoder has to integrate the deviations back into absolute phase, so small errors accumulate forward through time. A real effect, the wrong size to matter here.

Fig. — the smoothness/drift trade in the phase-derivative encoding. Re-anchoring to absolute phase more often (right side of each curve) buys back quality at the cost of the speckle the derivative encoding was meant to remove.

The crossover: resolution decides which encoding wins

The comparison above used the most fragile arrangement possible — one spectrogram bin per pixel. Barcodes solve exactly this problem by making each data cell several pixels wide. Doing the same here produces a clean, quantified crossover.

Pixels per binPhase-as-hue PESQGrayscale PESQWinner
1 × 11.062.59grayscale
2 × 21.733.30grayscale
4 × 43.303.53near tie
8 × 84.353.66phase-as-hue

Fig. — PESQ against pixels spent per spectrogram bin. Grayscale plateaus near 3.7 regardless of resolution, because guessed phase is its hard ceiling. Phase-carrying colour keeps climbing toward the digital-transparency numbers above it, once given enough paper per value to survive the channel.

This is the paper's central, defensible claim: it explains quantitatively why every prior printed-audio system (PhonoPaper included) went grayscale, and identifies the exact resolution at which that choice stops being correct. The price is capacity — at 300 dpi on A4, roughly four minutes of audio per page at 1×1 falls to about ten seconds at 4×4, before any error-correction overhead.

Status. All of the above is simulated channel damage, not a real printer and camera. It is a hypothesis about paper, generated by code that can now be pointed at a real print-and-scan test to check it. That physical run is the next step.

07 · The paper

Publication shape

ClaimFirst quantified study of phase-aware color spectrogram encoding through the physical print–scan channel. TypeEmpirical systems paper. Honest tier: workshop or mid-tier conference (ICASSP/EUSIPCO workshops, ISMIR late-breaking, or arXiv first). Acceptance is secondary to existence — stated project goal. Figure 1The founding image: two contrasting pieces of music side by side as phase-colored spectrograms — the "how does Mozart look" motivation, now serving as the hook. Skills fitAll required math is library calls (STFT, HSV conversion, PESQ). All required work is coding, pipeline building, experiment running — matching a strong-coder, math-light profile.

Known risks

  • Prior-art residue. Three independent search angles found no academic treatment of this exact question, but a final targeted literature pass at write-up time is mandatory.
  • Capacity disappointment. Physical capacity will be modest. Framed as a measured limit, not hidden, this is a result rather than a failure.
  • Phase fragility. Phase may prove too delicate for print. Even a negative result here is publishable: "phase does not survive the print–scan channel under X conditions; magnitude-plus-reconstructed-phase (Griffin-Lim) outperforms" is a real finding.
  • Scope creep. Route B (neural codec bits in a color barcode, minutes of audio per page) stays parked. It is one comparison row in the discussion section, not a second build.

08 · Sources

Reference shelf

  1. Log complex color for visual pattern recognition of total sound — US Patent 10,341,795 (2019). The digital prior art. Phase as hue, amplitude as brightness, claimed full reversibility.
  2. Phase representation based on HSV color model for acoustic classification with CNNs — IEEE (2021). Phase→HSV for classifiers.
  3. PhonoPaper — A. Zolotov (2014). The closest existing system; grayscale, no phase, no evaluation. Primary baseline to beat.
  4. StegaStamp: Invisible Hyperlinks in Physical Photographs — Tancik et al., CVPR (2019). Print–scan robustness as a serious research problem; learned distortion modeling.
  5. High Capacity Color Barcodes: Per Channel Data Encoding via Orientation Modulation — IEEE TIP (2011). Capacity baselines for paper as a data channel.
  6. Saving the Sonorine: Photovisual Audio Recovery — arXiv (2020). Precedent: audio from physical media via imaging is publishable.
  7. Audio-to-Image Encoding for Improved Voice Characteristic Detection — arXiv (2025). Recent RGB-channel audio encodings, classification-oriented.
  8. Single channel speech enhancement by colored spectrograms — arXiv (2023). Colored spectrograms in an enhancement pipeline.
  9. Printed audio format and photograph with encoded audio — US Patent 8,934,032. Kodak-era printed audio; historical context.
  10. SemantiCodec: An Ultra Low Bitrate Semantic Audio Codec — arXiv (2024). Parked Route B enabler; cite in discussion only.
